# Dates as dates {background-color="#0C234B"}

## Strings are not dates

```python
df = pd.read_csv("flow.csv")
df["datetime"].dtype        # object  -> these are strings
```

::: {.fragment}
Sorting gives you alphabetical order. `"2015-1-5"` and `"2015-01-05"` are
different values. You cannot subtract them.
:::

```python
df = pd.read_csv("flow.csv", parse_dates=["datetime"])
df = df.set_index("datetime").sort_index()
```

::: {.fragment}
Now you have a `DatetimeIndex`, and an entire API opens up.
:::

## Partial-string selection

The most useful thing in this deck.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 10
import pandas as pd, numpy as np

idx = pd.date_range("2005-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(len(idx)) / 58)) * 40, index=idx)

print(f'q.loc["2006"]              {len(q.loc["2006"]):5,} rows')
print(f'q.loc["2006-08"]           {len(q.loc["2006-08"]):5,} rows')
print(f'q.loc["2006-07":"2006-09"] {len(q.loc["2006-07":"2006-09"]):5,} rows')
```

::: {.fragment}
Note the slice is **inclusive of both ends** — the same `.loc` rule from Week 5,
and here it is exactly what you want.
:::

## `.dt` for a column that isn't the index

```python
levels["date"].dt.year
levels["date"].dt.month
levels["date"].dt.dayofyear
levels["date"].dt.quarter
```

::: {.fragment}
Use the index API when the dates *are* the index, and `.dt` when they are a
column you're grouping by. Long-format data — one row per measurement, well in a
column — usually wants `.dt`.
:::

## Your turn: select the monsoon

Pull July through September of 2006 out of a daily series.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_slice
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
idx = pd.date_range("2005-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(len(idx)) / 58)) * 40, index=idx)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_slice
monsoon = q.loc[______]
print(f"{len(monsoon)} days, from {monsoon.index.min():%b %d} to {monsoon.index.max():%b %d}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_slice"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

A slice of two partial strings. You don't need to know that September has 30
days — pandas works out the end of the month for you.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_slice"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
monsoon = q.loc["2006-07":"2006-09"]
```

92 days. `"2006-09"` as the end of a slice means *the end of September*, not the
first of September — which is the inclusive rule doing something genuinely
convenient for once.
:::
:::

# Resampling {background-color="#AB0520"}

## `groupby` for time

```python
q.resample("ME").mean()      # month end
q.resample("YE").sum()       # year end
q.resample("W").max()        # weekly
```

::: {.fragment}
7,305 daily values become 240 monthly or 20 annual ones.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Frequency strings changed in pandas 2.2.** It is `ME` and `YE` now, not `M`
and `Y`. Older tutorials use the old ones and you'll get a `FutureWarning` —
another instance of last week's theme.
:::

## The aggregation is a hydrology decision

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| average conditions | `.mean()` |
| total volume | `.sum()` |
| flood risk | `.max()` |
| a typical day, ignoring floods | `.median()` |

::: {.fragment}
Summing cfs over a month gives you **cfs-days**, which is a volume and a
perfectly good one — as long as the axis label says so.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Sabino Creek: the wettest year averaged 24.6 cfs, the driest 2.6. **A factor of
ten.** Any analysis built on "the average year" describes a year that does not
occur.
:::

## The water year

Hydrologists count years from **October 1 to September 30**.

::: {.incremental}
- A winter snowpack and the melt it feeds belong to the same year
- A calendar year splits them down the middle
- October 1 is the driest, least eventful moment in most of the western US
:::

::: {.fragment}
```python
q.resample("YE-SEP").sum()      # years ending 30 September
```
:::

::: {.fragment .due-notice}
Water year 2007 runs from **1 October 2006** to **30 September 2007**. It is
named for the year it *ends* in. Getting this wrong shifts your entire record by
three months.
:::

## Your turn: annual totals, two ways

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_wy
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
idx = pd.date_range("2005-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(len(idx)) / 58)) * 40, index=idx)
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_wy
calendar = q.resample(______).sum()
water_year = q.resample(______).sum()

print(f"calendar years: {len(calendar)}")
print(f"water years:    {len(water_year)}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_wy"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

Year-end is `"YE"`. To end the year in a different month, append the month's
three-letter abbreviation with a hyphen.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_wy"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
calendar = q.resample("YE").sum()
water_year = q.resample("YE-SEP").sum()
```

20 calendar years and 21 water years, from the same data. The extra one is a
stub: the record starts on 1 January 2005, which is already three months into
water year 2005, so that first bin is incomplete.

**Watch for that stub.** It will be the lowest bar on your chart, and it is an
artifact of where the record starts.
:::
:::

## Your turn: which water year?

A storm on **12 November 2013**. Which water year does it belong to, and how
would you compute that from a date?

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_wyear
import pandas as pd
d = pd.Timestamp("2013-11-12")
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_wyear
water_year = d.year + ______
print(f"{d:%d %B %Y} falls in water year {water_year}")
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_wyear"}
::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
## Hint

October, November, and December belong to the *next* water year. Everything
else belongs to its own calendar year. A comparison returns `True`, and `True`
is 1.
:::
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex_wyear"}
::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```python
water_year = d.year + (d.month >= 10)
```

Water year **2014**. November 2013 is already two months into it.

That one-liner works on a whole column too:
`df["date"].dt.year + (df["date"].dt.month >= 10)`. Adding a boolean to an
integer is idiomatic here, not a trick — `True` is 1 and it reads cleanly.
:::
:::

## Resample vs. groupby

```{pyodide}
#| edit: false
#| autorun: false
#| min-lines: 9
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
idx = pd.date_range("2005-01-01", "2024-12-31", freq="D")
q = pd.Series(np.abs(np.sin(np.arange(len(idx)) / 58)) * 40, index=idx)

print("resample('ME')          ->", len(q.resample("ME").mean()), "values (240 separate months)")
print("groupby(q.index.month)  ->", len(q.groupby(q.index.month).mean()), "values (all Januaries together)")
```

::: {.fragment}
**`resample` keeps time moving forward. `groupby` on a month number collapses
across years.** The second one is a *climatology* — the long-term average
January — and it is a different object entirely.
:::
